job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Ben Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in Yokohama and my day starts with a coffee and an AI assistant open on my second screen. I spend the morning on applications and a small freelance job, fixing a web shop for a ramen restaurant. In the afternoon I work on my own mobile game idea, and in the evening I go to the gym or play basketball with old school friends. It's a fairly good rhythm, but it's still not a job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was your internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did software engineering at a university in Tokyo and got a good result. I spent two months at a small game studio called Kitsune Works, testing builds and writing editor tools in Unity. My boss there, Ms Sato, liked my tools, but they couldn't hire anyone that year. I have a student loan, about eight weeks of savings, and my parents have said they'd help if I run short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I thought, and I'd keep working the way I do now. I use AI every day, so I know it's good but not magic. I'd tell friends that the hype always runs ahead of the product.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't solve my problem, which is that I missed the main hiring season and now I'm picking up scraps. Companies here hire new graduates in April, so I'm a bit out of sync. I'm not panicking, but I know the longer I wait the harder it gets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to about twelve companies a month, including mid-year hires at game studios and web firms. I'd keep the ramen shop job and look for two more small freelance clients. I'd also put 20,000 yen a month into an index fund, because I like building the habit early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly okay. Slightly impatient, but not low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of being out of sync with the hiring season?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because small habits are the only thing I control right now. I put in 20,000 yen from freelancing, and it makes me feel like I'm moving forward. If the job market turns, I'd at least have a small cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why invest while you're still without a salary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because small habits are the only thing I control right now. I put in 20,000 yen from freelancing, and it makes me feel like I'm moving forward. If the job market turns, I'd at least have a small cushion.

I'd keep working the way I do now, with AI every day.

Keep the ramen shop job and find **two more** small freelance clients.
Put **20,000 yen** a month into an index fund.

fieldNote: He's uneasy rather than anxious because freelance income and family backing are real.

Put 20,000 yen a month into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting and risky at the same time. Coding and testing are on the card by name, so juniors like me will have a different job. I'd tell friends to learn to direct AI, not just use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the junior programmer who only writes simple functions is the first to go. What's left is someone who understands the product, the players and the whole system. I like that, because my game idea needs exactly that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build two or three small apps with AI in public and put them on an app store, to show I can ship. I'd apply to teams that want product-minded engineers, and I'd take a short course in game design and monetisation. I'd also keep freelancing, since clients pay for outcomes, not for job titles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, with a small pit of worry. I'd call it nervous excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the apps need to earn to count as a success?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go solo or with two friends, and form a tiny studio. It's risky, but with AI tools three people can do what ten did. And I'd keep my parents' house as a base until it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the junior jobs are really gone, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go solo or with two friends, and form a tiny studio. It's risky, but with AI tools three people can do what ten did. And I'd keep my parents' house as a base until it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and companies and governments should say so openly. I'd also say it doesn't help to freeze. Two years is short, but it's long enough to try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. If AI does nearly all thinking work within two years, what does a junior game programmer even do? I'd guess a few studios survive on creativity and taste, but the rest drop quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast: ship two apps in three months, sell small services to local shops, and take every freelance client. I'd put my freelance income into an index fund and keep a bigger cash buffer. I'd also ask my parents whether I can stay home for at least two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but sharp. It's like the last minutes of a match, where you try everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kenji, your friend with the big firm job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't count on the badge, because big firms may cut their new hires first. He'd laugh, then probably go quiet. We'd end up shooting hoops and not talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think you'd still be good at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Taste, I guess. Knowing what makes a game fun, what makes a menu easy for players. AI can make a thousand levels, but someone still has to say which one is good.

I'd say freezing doesn't help; two years is enough to try things.

steps.text: Ship two apps within three months
Sell AI booking services to local shops
Build a larger cash buffer from freelance pay
Stay at my parents' home for two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good window, and I'd tell people to start experimenting now. I'd say the companies that adapt will hire, and the ones that wait will shrink. I'd also say people should be kind to each other, since it's a lot of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. If I land a job this year, I'd get four years to grow into something that's hard to replace, like a producer or product lead. And if not, I have the freelance and app income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job at a studio that uses AI heavily and ask for projects that touch design and players. I'd invest a quarter of my pay, mostly in broad index funds, and keep building my own game on weekends. I'd also learn some game business basics, like budgets and publishing deals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of drive. I like having a few years to play with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know if the window was closing faster than the card says?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When my freelance clients start doing the work themselves with AI, and when mid-year hires disappear. I'd see it in the job boards before the news. If that happens I'd move my money and my plans a year earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a quarter of your pay actually buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me options, which is the point. If I can live on three quarters, then in four years I'd have close to a year of expenses saved. That feels like a healthy amount of freedom.

say: I'd say five years is a **good window**, and people should start experimenting now.
I'd add that people should be kind to each other, since it's a lot of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and it's a good time to be curious. I'd tell friends to learn something they enjoy, because enjoyment is what keeps people learning. I'd say the future of work will be more varied than the headlines say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly relaxed. In ten years I could run my own small studio, and I'd have time to do it well. The robots arrive later, so physical hardware and arcades could even be a niche for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job, learn the industry, then spin off my own team around year three. I'd invest steadily and buy a small flat near Yokohama in my late twenties. I'd keep teaching myself new tools, like a new engine every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm. Ten years sounds like enough for a few mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistakes are you expecting to make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably hiring the wrong friend, or building a game nobody wants. I did the second one already, in a university project, and it taught me to test with real players early. I'd rather fail small and soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want something from your family in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just space to try. My mum worries about stability, and my dad is more relaxed. If they trust me, I can be bolder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, mainly because the people I love might not be ready. What would help is fast, cheap retraining, a safety net that doesn't depend on a company, and clear honesty from the government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd do on my last free day before the change. I'd go to a basketball court with Kenji and the old friends, and play until dark. Whatever comes, I'd like to have a night on the court with my old friends.

headlineQuote: Whatever comes, I'd like to have a night on the court with my old friends.
portrait: Ben is a **software engineering** graduate in Yokohama who missed the April hiring season and has no offer yet.
He uses AI daily, freelances for a ramen restaurant, and builds small apps and a game idea at home.
He is pragmatic about politics and blames no one in particular, mostly the **hiring calendar**.
Mood runs from uneasy at the plateau to **anxious** at two years, and calm at five and ten.
His strengths are taste, shipping small things, and a family that gives him space to try.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case, mainly because the people he loves might not be ready.
whatWouldHelp: Fast, cheap **retraining** and a safety net that doesn't depend on a company.
Honesty from the government about what is coming.
